catalog_quote: [p.108] ...while long vowels are always stressed in Hawaiian, short vowels are only stressed contingently depending on their position in the metrical structure... [p.110] These state that stress is typically perceived on a penultimate short vowel as in [liˈona] liona ‘lion’. A word like [ˈloina] loina ‘custom’ violates this rule and motivates the analysis of /oi/ as a diphthong. ... in Hawaiian, heavy syllables always receive stress on their first vowel ... [p.111] The phonology of Hawaiian is weight-sensitive... Syllables containing a long vowel or a diphthong (or both) are ‘heavy’ and all heavy syllables are stressed, whereas syllables containing a single short vowel are ‘light’ and may or may not be stressed, depending on metrical position... Deciding source is a 2018 JIPA Illustration by the scholar whose Oxford theses are the main modern work on Hawaiian stress; nothing in Glottolog's list (pedagogical/older grammars, Schütz 1981) outranks it for stress. sources.citation: Schütz, Albert J. 2010. Measures and morphemes: a functional approach to Hawaiian accent. In John Bowden, Nikolaus P. Himmelmann & Malcolm Ross (eds.), A journey through Austronesian and Papuan linguistic and cultural space: papers in honour of Andrew K. Pawley (Pacific Linguistics 615), 405-421. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics. Open Access CC BY-SA 4.0, hdl 1885/146763.
sources.quote: p.406: of Hayes's Fijian-type rules '(a) If the final syllable is light, main stress falls on the penult. (b) If the final syllable is heavy, main stress falls on the final syllable. (c) Secondary stress falls on remaining heavy syllables, and on every other light syllable...' Schütz says 'statements (a), (b), and the first half of (c) are valid. The incorrect portion is the phrase in (c) referring to alternating syllables' (pùlelehúa, makùahíne vs ‘èlemakúle). fn.3: 'the last measure in the word (phrase) is emphasised to mark its end'. p.409: within a measure 'Accent occurs on: 1. a syllable
sources.locator: pp.406-407 (sec. 2), fn.3 p.407, p.409 (three accent principles, even/uneven measures, Table 1)
sources.note: The Hawaiian accent specialist's fullest statement; explicitly validates final-heavy-else-penult primary stress and all-heavy secondary stress while rejecting alternating light-syllable secondary stress — exactly the hedge our 'weight-hedged' coding encodes. fetched sources now; should be added to the record's sources.
